title: Resonance & damping
examples: What makes a swing go higher when you push at just the right time?
How does air resistance affect the vibration of a guitar string?
Can you explain the difference between damping and resonance?

explain.say: Today we are learning about resonance and damping in waves. Resonance happens when a driving force matches a natural frequency. This causes the amplitude of vibration to increase greatly. Consider a simple pendulum swinging back and forth.

The natural frequency is the frequency at which an object vibrates naturally. This depends on the object's physical properties. For example, a longer pendulum has a lower natural frequency. Think about plucking a guitar string.

Damping is the dissipation of energy from an oscillating system. This usually happens due to resistance like air friction. A common example is a bouncing ball losing energy over time. This effect slows the oscillations down.

We see two main types of damping. Viscous damping is proportional to velocity, like thick oil resistance. Another type is damping proportional to the square of the velocity. Think about air resistance on a falling object.

In a real-life scenario, car shock absorbers use damping. They are designed to absorb the energy from the car's suspension. This prevents the car from bouncing uncontrollably after hitting a bump. They control the oscillation.

A common mistake is assuming damping always stops all motion. In reality, damping only reduces the amplitude over time. If the driving force is removed, the object will eventually stop. Remember that damping reduces energy, not necessarily motion instantly.

items: It does not stop it immediately.

draw.text: Damping reduces amplitude, not motion instantly

faq.q: What is the difference between natural frequency and forced frequency?
faq.a: The natural frequency is the frequency an object vibrates at by itself. The forced frequency is the frequency of the external force pushing it. Asks: What is an object's natural rate of vibration? What is the driving frequency?
asks: What is the object's own frequency?
How is the natural frequency determined?

faq.q: Does damping always cause the object to stop moving?
faq.a: No, damping only reduces the amplitude of the vibration over time. If there is still an external force, the object will continue to move, just with a smaller swing. Asks: Does damping stop all movement? Will the object stop if I keep pushing it?
asks: How does damping affect continuous motion?
Is stopping motion the same as damping?

faq.q: Which type of damping is most common in everyday life?
faq.a: Viscous damping is often modeled as the most common type. This type is proportional to the velocity, similar to moving through honey. Asks: What is damping like in water? Is air resistance viscous?
asks: What is the simplest model for damping?
Can air resistance be modeled as viscous?

faq.q: What causes resonance in a bridge?
faq.a: Resonance occurs when the frequency of an external force matches the bridge's natural frequency. This can cause dangerously large vibrations. Asks: Why do bridges shake in the wind? What frequency causes resonance?
asks: What makes a bridge vibrate strongly?
What frequency should we avoid for bridges?

faq.q: How can engineers prevent resonance in structures?
faq.a: Engineers use damping mechanisms, like tuned mass dampers, to absorb vibrational energy. They aim to shift the natural frequency away from expected driving frequencies. Asks: How do we make buildings safe from wind? What is a damper?
asks: What stops buildings from shaking too much?

facts: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency.
Damping causes the amplitude of oscillation to decrease over time.
Viscous damping force is proportional to the velocity (F ∝ v).
A pendulum's natural frequency depends on its length and gravity.

quiz.say: A guitar string vibrates at its natural frequency. If you pluck it with a force that vibrates at the same frequency, what happens?
quiz.why: When the driving force matches the natural frequency, resonance occurs, increasing amplitude.

wrong.0: Resonance involves matching frequencies, not changing the frequency itself.
wrong.2: While very high amplitude can cause breakage, the immediate result of resonance is increased amplitude, not guaranteed breakage.
wrong.3: Resonance adds energy to the system, causing larger vibrations, not stopping them.

quiz.say: A mass attached to a spring oscillates. If air resistance is present, what is the effect on the amplitude?
quiz.why: Air resistance causes damping, which dissipates energy and reduces the maximum swing size.

wrong.1: While the period change is small, damping does slightly affect the period, and the primary effect is amplitude decay.
wrong.2: Damping causes the system to lose energy, which generally leads to a slight decrease in frequency, not a steady increase.
wrong.3: Damping causes the envelope of the oscillation to decay, making it non-sinusoidal over time.

quiz.say: If a system has a natural frequency of ten hertz, and an external force drives it at twenty hertz, what is the expected motion?
quiz.why: Since the driving frequency does not match the natural frequency, the system vibrates, but the amplitude will decay due to damping.

wrong.0: Resonance only happens when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency.
wrong.1: The system continues to oscillate because the driving force is still applied, even if it is not resonant.
wrong.2: Infinite increase only happens at resonance, not when the frequencies are mismatched.
